clinicalPearls: The core ataxic syndrome is gait impairment, scanning (unclear) speech, blurred vision from nystagmus, limb incoordination, and tremor on movement, reflecting disease of the cerebellum and its afferent/efferent pathways including the spinocerebellar and frontopontocerebellar tracts (p.3533).

True cerebellar ataxia is an unsteady, imbalanced gait without vertigo, light-headedness, or sense of movement; vestibular/labyrinthine disorders by contrast produce gait disturbance accompanied by prominent dizziness (p.3533).

Sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia can mimic cerebellar imbalance but is distinguished because instability worsens markedly when visual input is removed (positive Romberg sign); rarely proximal leg weakness also mimics cerebellar disease (p.3533).

The tempo and pattern of onset guide etiology: gradual, bilateral, symmetric progression points to genetic, metabolic, immune, or toxic causes, whereas focal unilateral signs with headache and depressed consciousness, ipsilateral cranial nerve palsies, and contralateral weakness suggest a space-occupying cerebellar lesion (p.3533).

Acute, reversible symmetric ataxias commonly follow intoxication with alcohol, phenytoin, lithium, or barbiturates and exposures such as toluene, gasoline/glue sniffing, methyl mercury, or bismuth (p.3533-3534).

Subacute symmetric ataxia raises suspicion of alcoholic-nutritional vermal degeneration (thiamine/B12 deficiency), paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, immune-mediated ataxia, or a prion disorder (p.3533-3534).
Friedreich's ataxia is the most common inherited ataxia, accounting for about half of all hereditary ataxias, and is autosomal recessive (p.3536).

Friedreich's ataxia features onset before age 25 with progressive staggering gait, areflexia, extensor plantar responses, loss of vibratory/proprioceptive sensation, and frequently pes cavus and scoliosis (p.3536).

Among the dominant ataxias, the polyglutamine SCAs (SCA1, SCA2, SCA3/Machado-Joseph, SCA6, SCA7, SCA17) arise from expanded CAG triplet repeats; genotype, not phenotype, is the diagnostic gold standard because clinical pictures overlap (p.3534).

Retinal pigmentary degeneration (blue-yellow color blindness progressing to macular degeneration and visual loss) is the distinguishing feature of SCA7 among the spinocerebellar ataxias (p.3535-3536).

Episodic ataxia type 1 causes brief (minutes-long) attacks of ataxia with myokymia and nystagmus, while type 2 produces longer attacks lasting hours to days; type 2 stems from CACNA1A mutations (the same calcium-channel gene as SCA6 and familial hemiplegic migraine) (p.3536).
A treatable mimic to always exclude in chronic symmetric gait ataxia is hypothyroidism; infectious causes to consider include meningovascular syphilis/tabes dorsalis and Lyme disease (p.3534).
harrison.pathophysiology: Ataxia results from dysfunction of the cerebellum and the pathways connecting it to the rest of the nervous system, including the spinocerebellar tracts and the frontopontocerebellar pathway arising in the rostral frontal lobe. In the inherited polyglutamine spinocerebellar ataxias, expanded CAG triplet repeats produce mutant ataxin proteins with abnormally long polyglutamine tracts (generally toxic beyond ~40 glutamines); these proteins misfold into beta-pleated aggregates, are abnormally transported into the nucleus, bind and impair other polyglutamine proteins such as TATA-binding protein and CREB-binding protein, disrupt the ubiquitin-proteasome protein-turnover system, and trigger neuronal apoptosis, yielding a relatively disease-specific pattern of neuronal loss and gliosis. Longer repeats correlate with earlier onset and more aggressive disease across generations (anticipation). In Friedreich's ataxia, an expanded GAA repeat in the first intron of the frataxin gene silences frataxin expression; frataxin is a mitochondrial protein involved in iron homeostasis, so its loss causes mitochondrial iron accumulation, deficiency of iron-sulfur cluster enzymes, reduced ATP production, oxidative injury, and irreversible cell death, with predominant degeneration of the spinal cord (spinocerebellar tracts, lateral corticospinal tracts, posterior columns), dorsal root ganglia, and peripheral nerves.
additionalDifferentials: Vestibular/labyrinthine disorder (gait disturbance with vertigo, distinguished from cerebellar ataxia)
Sensory ataxia from peripheral neuropathy or posterior column disease (Romberg-positive)
Proximal leg weakness mimicking cerebellar imbalance
Toxic/drug-induced cerebellar ataxia (alcohol, phenytoin, lithium, barbiturates, chemotherapeutic agents such as fluorouracil and paclitaxel)
Alcoholic-nutritional cerebellar degeneration with thiamine/B12 deficiency
Cerebellar mass (infarction, hemorrhage, abscess, glioma, metastasis, subdural hematoma)
Congenital malformations: Chiari malformation, Dandy-Walker posterior fossa cyst
infectionMimics: Acute viral cerebellitis (e.g., poliovirus, coxsackievirus, echovirus, Epstein-Barr virus)
Postinfectious cerebellar ataxia, especially after varicella (reversible gait ataxia and mild dysarthria)
Meningovascular syphilis and tabes dorsalis (posterior column/spinocerebellar degeneration)
AIDS-related progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy or CNS lymphoma presenting as a focal cerebellar syndrome
nonInfectiousMimics: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (anti-Yo with breast/ovarian cancer, anti-PQ calcium-channel antibody with small-cell lung cancer, anti-Tr with Hodgkin's disease; anti-Ri opsoclonus-myoclonus with breast/lung cancer and neuroblastoma)
Anti-GAD65 antibody-associated progressive ataxia without underlying cancer
Gluten/antigliadin antibody-associated ataxia (HLA DQB1*0201, may have villus atrophy on small-bowel biopsy)
Vitamin E deficiency states (abetalipoproteinemia/Bassen-Kornzweig and ataxia with vitamin E deficiency)
additionalInvestigations: MRI/CT of brain and posterior fossa to detect cerebellar atrophy or mass lesions; spinal cord MRI shows atrophy in Friedreich's ataxia
Genetic (genotype) testing for triplet-repeat expansions, now the diagnostic gold standard for the inherited ataxias
Serum vitamin B1, B12, and vitamin E levels
Paraneoplastic and autoimmune antibody panels (anti-Yo, anti-PQ calcium channel, anti-Tr, anti-Ri, anti-GAD65, antigliadin/antiendomysium)
CSF examination, including testing for syphilis and for evidence of acute viral infection
Lyme disease and Legionella antibody titers
ECG/echocardiography in Friedreich's ataxia (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, conduction defects) and glucose testing for associated diabetes mellitus
Serum alpha-fetoprotein and immunoglobulin levels in suspected ataxia-telangiectasia
redFlags: Acute focal ataxia with headache, depressed consciousness, and ipsilateral pontine/cranial nerve signs suggesting cerebellar infarction or hemorrhage with brainstem compression

Rapidly worsening focal cerebellar signs raising concern for posterior fossa hematoma, abscess, or tumor at risk of rostral (tentorial) or downward (foramen magnum/tonsillar) herniation, which can be devastating and may require emergent surgical decompression
Subacute progressive ataxia as the presenting feature of an occult malignancy (paraneoplastic syndrome)
Cardiac symptoms in Friedreich's ataxia (cardiomegaly, hypertrophy, conduction defects), since cardiac involvement occurs in about 90% of patients
Recurrent pulmonary infections and lymphoreticular malignancy risk in ataxia-telangiectasia
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends on cause: several acquired ataxias (intoxications, postinfectious ataxia, hypothyroidism, vitamin deficiencies) are reversible, whereas the inherited degenerative ataxias progress relentlessly. In Machado-Joseph disease (SCA3) deficits invariably progress to death from debilitation within about 15 years of onset (especially types I and II), with intellect usually preserved. Friedreich's ataxia has a median age of death around 35 years, and women have a significantly better prognosis than men. Larger triplet-repeat expansions correlate with earlier onset and more aggressive disease, and anticipation produces earlier, more severe disease in successive generations.
pitfalls: Mislabeling vestibular or sensory (proprioceptive) imbalance as cerebellar ataxia; absence of vertigo and a positive Romberg sign help distinguish them.
Overlooking readily treatable and reversible causes such as hypothyroidism, vitamin E/B1/B12 deficiency, and intoxications.
Relying on clinical phenotype alone to classify inherited ataxias, since SCA phenotypes overlap and genotype is the diagnostic gold standard.
In Machado-Joseph disease type I, the stiff broad-based lurching gait results from spasticity rather than true ataxia and lacks truncal titubation, which can be misread.
Failing to recognize an acute focal cerebellar lesion as a neurosurgical emergency because of herniation risk.
Forgetting that some SCAs have prominent non-cerebellar features (e.g., retinal degeneration in SCA7, parkinsonism/extrapyramidal signs in SCA1/SCA2, peripheral neuropathy in MJD type III).
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal severity score is given; etiologic and temporal frameworks are used instead. Cerebellar ataxia is categorized as symmetric/progressive versus focal/ipsilateral, each subdivided by tempo into acute (hours to days), subacute (days to weeks), or chronic (months to years) per Table 450-1. Inherited ataxias are classified genomically by mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant (SCAs, DRPLA, episodic ataxias), autosomal recessive (Friedreich's ataxia, ataxia-telangiectasia, RFC1-related CANVAS), and mitochondrial. Machado-Joseph disease is further graded into clinical types I (ALS-parkinsonism-dystonia), II (ataxic, most common), and III (ataxic-amyotrophic).
management: Identification and correction of reversible causes: thiamine, vitamin B12 and vitamin E repletion, thyroid hormone replacement for hypothyroidism, and withdrawal of offending drugs or toxins such as alcohol, phenytoin or lithium
Immunotherapy for immune-mediated ataxia and treatment of any underlying tumour in paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration
Neurosurgical management of a space-occupying cerebellar lesion causing focal signs and raised intracranial pressure
Supportive neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and mobility and communication aids for the incurable degenerative ataxias
Symptomatic treatment of associated features such as tremor, spasticity and bladder dysfunction
Genetic counselling and family testing for inherited triplet-repeat and other hereditary ataxias
Multidisciplinary follow-up with monitoring of swallowing, respiration and nutrition as disability progresses
